questions.text: Which estimate is reasonable?

options.A: $1\times10^{-3}\,\text{kg}$ for the mass of a grain of sand
options.B: $1\times10^{-2}\,\text{m}^3$ for the volume of a tennis ball
options.C: $1\times10^{0}\,\text{J}$ for the work done lifting an apple from waist height to head height
options.D: $1\times10^{4}\,\text{W}$ for the power of a light bulb in a house

questions.explanation:
Apple mass ≈ 0.1 kg, lift ≈ 0.6–1 m: $W=mgh\approx0.1\times9.81\times0.8\approx1\,\text{J}$. Reasonable.

Sand grain ≈ $10^{-6}$ kg or less; tennis ball volume ≈ $1.5\times10^{-4}\,\text{m}^3$; bulb ≈ 10–100 W.

Tempting A: 1 g is far too heavy for a sand grain.

questions.text: What is the symbol for the SI base unit of temperature?
questions.explanation:
The SI base unit of temperature is the kelvin, symbol K (no degree sign).

Tempting D: '°K' is an obsolete, incorrect notation.

questions.text: Which statement about systematic errors is **not** correct?

options.A: A systematic error can be caused by using an incorrectly calibrated instrument.
options.B: One particular type of systematic error can affect all the measurements by the same amount.
options.C: The effect of a systematic error can be reduced by repeating and averaging the measurements.
options.D: Zero error is a type of systematic error.

questions.explanation:
Systematic errors shift every reading in the same way, so averaging repeated readings does not reduce them; averaging only reduces random errors. So C is incorrect.

Tempting B: it is true — a zero error offsets all readings equally.

questions.text:
An object is moving with an initial velocity of $4.0\,\text{m s}^{-1}$ to the right. The velocity of the object changes so that its final velocity is $3.0\,\text{m s}^{-1}$ downwards, as shown.

Which arrow represents the change in velocity of the object?

options.A: Arrow pointing down and to the right
options.B: Arrow pointing down and to the left
options.C: Arrow pointing up and to the right
options.D: Arrow pointing up and to the left

questions.explanation:
$\Delta v = v_f - v_i = (3.0\text{ down}) + (4.0\text{ left})$. The resultant points down and to the left (magnitude 5.0 m s$^{-1}$).

Tempting A: that is $v_f + v_i$, adding instead of subtracting.

questions.text:
A car travels anticlockwise along a horizontal circular road of radius 12 m, as shown.

The car takes a time of 4.0 s to move from position P to position Q.

What is the magnitude of the average velocity of the car for the journey from P to Q?
questions.explanation:
P and Q are 90° apart on the circle, so displacement = $\sqrt{12^2+12^2}=17.0$ m. Average velocity = $17.0/4.0=4.2\,\text{m s}^{-1}$.

Tempting D: uses the 270° anticlockwise arc length ($56.5$ m) giving average speed.

questions.text:
The water surface in a deep well is 78.0 m below the top of the well. A person at the top of the well drops a heavy stone down the well.

Air resistance is negligible. The speed of sound in the air is $330\,\text{m s}^{-1}$.

What is the time interval between the person dropping the stone and hearing it hitting the water?
questions.explanation:
Fall: $t_1=\sqrt{2h/g}=\sqrt{2\times78.0/9.81}=3.99$ s. Sound: $t_2=78.0/330=0.236$ s. Total $=4.22$ s.

Tempting B: ignores the sound travel time.

questions.text: Which statement is **not** a requirement of a pair of forces that obey Newton’s third law of motion?

options.A: The forces act in opposite directions.
options.B: The forces act on different objects.
options.C: The forces act on objects in contact.
options.D: The forces are of equal magnitude.

questions.explanation:
Third-law pairs are equal, opposite, of the same type and act on different bodies. Contact is not required, e.g. gravitational attraction between Earth and Moon.

Tempting B: acting on different objects is essential.

questions.text:
A child of mass 20 kg stands on the rough surface of a sledge of mass 40 kg. The sledge can slide on a horizontal frictionless surface.

One end of a rope is attached to the sledge. The rope passes around a fixed frictionless pole, and the other end of the rope is held by the child, as shown.

The rope is horizontal. The child pulls on the rope with a horizontal force of 12 N. This causes the child and the sledge to move with equal acceleration towards the pole.

What is the frictional force between the child and the sledge?
questions.explanation:
Tension 12 N acts on both child and sledge towards the pole: total 24 N on 60 kg, so $a=0.40\,\text{m s}^{-2}$. Child: $12 - f = 20\times0.40=8$, so $f=4.0$ N (friction on child acts away from pole).

Tempting C: 8.0 N is the child's net force, not the friction.

questions.text:
A stone S and a foam rubber ball R are identical spheres of equal volume. They are released from rest at time $t = 0$ and fall vertically through the air. Both reach terminal velocity.

Which graph best shows the variation with time $t$ of the speed $v$ of the stone and of the rubber ball?

options.A: Same initial gradient; R reaches higher terminal speed than S
options.B: Same initial gradient; S reaches higher terminal speed than R
options.C: Single curve for R and S together
options.D: S rises faster initially; both reach same terminal speed

questions.explanation: Initially both have speed zero, so no drag: both accelerate at $g$, giving the same initial gradient. Terminal velocity occurs when drag equals weight. The stone is heavier, and since the spheres have identical shape, the stone needs a larger drag, so a higher speed, to balance its weight. So S has the higher terminal speed: graph B. D wrongly gives equal terminal speeds and different initial gradients.

questions.text:
Two balls X and Y are moving towards each other with speeds of $5\,\text{m s}^{-1}$ and $15\,\text{m s}^{-1}$ respectively.

They make a perfectly elastic head-on collision and ball Y moves to the right with a speed of $7\,\text{m s}^{-1}$.

What is the speed and direction of ball X after the collision?
questions.explanation: For a perfectly elastic collision, relative speed of approach = relative speed of separation. Approach: $5+15=20\,\text{m s}^{-1}$. Taking right as positive, $v_Y - v_X = 20$, so $7 - v_X = 20$, $v_X = -13\,\text{m s}^{-1}$, i.e. $13\,\text{m s}^{-1}$ to the left. Option A comes from wrongly subtracting $7$ from... a mistaken difference of speeds.

questions.text:
Two forces form a couple.

Which statement describes the two forces?

options.A: They are in the same direction.
options.B: They are perpendicular to each other.
options.D: They pass through the same point.

questions.explanation: A couple is a pair of forces equal in magnitude, opposite in direction, acting along parallel lines that do not coincide. They produce rotation but no resultant force. So they have the same magnitude. D is wrong: forces through the same point produce no torque.

questions.text:
A uniform rod is attached by a hinge at one end to a wall. The other end of the rod is supported by a wire so that the rod is horizontal and in equilibrium.

Which arrow shows the direction of the force on the rod from the hinge?
questions.explanation: Three forces act: weight at the centre, wire tension at the free end, hinge force. For equilibrium, they must pass through one point: the weight's line meets the wire directly above the midpoint. The hinge force must point from the hinge to that point: up and away from the wall (right). Also, the tension pulls the rod toward the wall, so the hinge must push right. A ignores the horizontal component.

questions.text:
A diving board of length $5.0\,\text{m}$ is hinged at one end and supported $2.0\,\text{m}$ from this end by a spring of spring constant $10\,\text{kN m}^{-1}$. A child of mass $40\,\text{kg}$ stands at the far end of the board.

What is the extra compression of the spring caused by the child standing on the end of the board?
questions.explanation: Moments about hinge: $F\times2.0 = 40\times9.81\times5.0$, so $F = 981\,\text{N}$. Compression $x = F/k = 981/10000 = 0.098\,\text{m} = 9.8\,\text{cm}$. D comes from using $g\approx10$ incorrectly with wrong ratio or forgetting units scaling; A from omitting $g$-related factors.

questions.text:
A granite rock at the surface of the Earth has density $\rho$. The rock is transported to the surface of another planet.

The acceleration of free fall on the surface of the other planet is twice that on the surface of the Earth.

What is the density of the rock on the other planet?
questions.explanation: Density = mass/volume. Neither mass nor volume depends on gravitational field strength, so density remains $\rho$. C confuses mass with weight, which doubles.

questions.text:
A closed U-shaped tube contains a stationary liquid of density $\rho$. One side of the tube contains a gas at pressure $p_1$ and the other side contains a gas at pressure $p_2$, as shown.

The acceleration of free fall is $g$.

Which equation is correct?
questions.explanation: The liquid surface on the $p_1$ side is at depth $y$ below the top; on the $p_2$ side at depth $z$. The difference in liquid levels is $y-z$, with the $p_2$ side higher. At the level of the lower surface, pressures are equal: $p_1 = p_2 + \rho g(y-z)$, so $p_1 - p_2 = \rho g(y-z)$. A and B ignore the gas pressure on the other side.

questions.text: Which product of two quantities is equal to power?
questions.explanation: Power $P = W/t = Fs/t = Fv$. So force × velocity equals power. A gives work done, not power; C should be division by time, not multiplication.

questions.text:
Researchers have developed a new type of filament lamp with an efficiency of 40%. Old-type filament lamps have an efficiency of 5.0%. The two types of lamp produce the same useful output power.

What is the ratio $\dfrac{\text{input power to new type of lamp}}{\text{input power to old type of lamp}}$?
questions.explanation:
Input power = useful output / efficiency. With equal output P: ratio = (P/0.40)/(P/0.050) = 0.050/0.40 = 0.125 ≈ 0.13.

D (8.0) is the inverse ratio, old to new.

questions.text:
A student attempts to derive the formula for kinetic energy $E_\text{K}$. She begins by considering an object of mass $m$ which is initially at rest. A constant force $F$ applied to the object causes it to accelerate to final velocity $v$ in displacement $s$. The kinetic energy gained by the object is equal to the work done on the object by the force $F$.

Which equation would the student **not** need in order to derive the formula for $E_\text{K}$?
questions.explanation:
Derivation: W = Fs = mas, and with u = 0, as = v²/2, so E_K = ½mv². This uses F = ma, W = Fs and v² = u² + 2as. E = ½Fs is not needed (it is the form for elastic energy with varying force).

D might seem unnecessary but it links as to v².

questions.text:
A metal wire obeys Hooke’s law and has a Young modulus of $2.0 \times 10^{11}\,\text{Pa}$. The wire has an original length of $1.6\,\text{m}$ and a diameter of $0.48 \times 10^{-3}\,\text{m}$.

What is the spring constant of the wire?
questions.explanation:
k = F/x = EA/L. A = π(0.24×10⁻³)² = 1.81×10⁻⁷ m². k = 2.0×10¹¹ × 1.81×10⁻⁷ / 1.6 = 2.3×10⁴ N m⁻¹.

D uses the diameter instead of radius in the area (4× too large).

questions.text:
A wire is being stretched by a tensile force.

Which statement about the elastic limit **must** be correct?

options.A: The deformation is plastic after the elastic limit has been reached.
options.B: The deformation is plastic until the elastic limit is reached.
options.C: The extension is proportional to the tensile force after the elastic limit has been reached.
options.D: The extension is proportional to the tensile force until the elastic limit is reached.

questions.explanation:
The elastic limit is the point beyond which the wire no longer returns to its original length, so deformation beyond it is plastic.

D is tempting but proportionality holds only to the limit of proportionality, which may be before the elastic limit.

questions.text: Which statement is correct for **all** types of progressive wave?

options.A: The distance from a peak to the next trough is equal to a wavelength.
options.B: They can be demonstrated in ripple tanks.
options.D: They transfer energy from one position to another.

questions.explanation:
All progressive waves transfer energy without net transfer of matter. Peak to next trough is half a wavelength; EM waves need no atoms and are not ripple-tank waves.

C fails for electromagnetic waves.

questions.text:
A transverse water wave is moving along the surface of some water. This causes a ball to move vertically without moving horizontally as it floats upon the surface. At one instant, the ball is at the position shown.

The wave has a frequency of $0.20\,\text{Hz}$ and an amplitude of $0.70\,\text{m}$. The distance between a trough and an adjacent peak is $2.4\,\text{m}$.

What is the distance travelled by the ball in a time of $20\,\text{s}$?
questions.explanation:
Period T = 1/0.20 = 5 s, so 20 s = 4 oscillations. Each oscillation the ball moves 4A = 2.8 m vertically. Distance = 4 × 2.8 = 11.2 m.

D wrongly uses the horizontal 2.4 m (wave distance), which the ball does not travel.

questions.text:
A sound wave travels from left to right across a room. The variation with distance across the room of the displacement of the air molecules at one instant is shown.

At which distance will the air pressure be lowest?
questions.explanation:
Positive displacement = right. At D, molecules to the left are displaced left (negative) and those to the right displaced right (positive), so they move apart: a rarefaction, lowest pressure.

At B molecules either side move towards B: compression (highest pressure). A and C are zero-strain points.

questions.text:
A source emits a sound wave of a single frequency. The Doppler effect causes a different frequency of sound to be heard by a stationary observer.

What is a requirement for the Doppler effect to occur?

options.A: a source that is moving as it produces the sound wave
options.B: a source that produces a polarised sound wave
options.C: a source that produces a sound wave of changing amplitude
options.D: a source that produces a sound wave of changing frequency

questions.explanation:
With a stationary observer, the observed frequency changes only if the source moves relative to the observer, compressing or stretching the wavefronts.

D describes an actual emitted frequency change, not the Doppler effect.

questions.text:
An electromagnetic wave in free space has a frequency of $2.5\times10^{14}\,\text{Hz}$.

Which region of the electromagnetic spectrum includes this frequency?
questions.explanation:
Wavelength $\lambda=c/f=3.0\times10^8/2.5\times10^{14}=1.2\times10^{-6}\,\text{m}=1.2\,\mu\text{m}$. This is longer than visible light (400–700 nm) but much shorter than microwaves (mm–cm), so it is infrared.

Ultraviolet is tempting but UV wavelengths are shorter than 400 nm.

questions.text:
Two polarising filters are placed next to each other so that their planes are parallel.

The first polarising filter has its transmission axis at an angle of 50° to the vertical.

The second polarising filter has its transmission axis at an angle of 20° to the vertical. The angle between the transmission axes of the two polarising filters is 30°.

A beam of vertically polarised light of intensity $8.0\,\text{W m}^{-2}$ is incident normally on the first polarising filter.

What is the intensity of the light that is transmitted from the second polarising filter?
questions.explanation:
Malus's law $I=I_0\cos^2\theta$ applied twice.

First filter: $8.0\cos^2 50°=8.0\times0.413=3.31\,\text{W m}^{-2}$.

Second filter: $3.31\cos^2 30°=3.31\times0.75=2.5\,\text{W m}^{-2}$.

C ($2.9$) comes from using $\cos$ instead of $\cos^2$ incorrectly or using 20°; only the double $\cos^2$ gives 2.5.

questions.text:
A stationary wave on a stretched string is set up between two points P and T.

Which statement about the stationary wave is correct?

options.A: Point R is at a node.
options.B: Points Q and S vibrate in phase.
options.C: The distance between P and T is three wavelengths.
options.D: The wave transfers energy from P to T.

questions.explanation:
The diagram shows three loops between P and T. Q and S are antinodes in the first and third loops; they are separated by two loops (one wavelength), so they move in phase.

R is an antinode, not a node; three loops = 1.5 wavelengths; stationary waves transfer no net energy. A is tempting because R is drawn at a low point, but it is a displacement maximum.

questions.text:
A bar vibrates with frequency $f$ to produce water waves in a ripple tank.

The waves pass through a gap of width $x$ in a barrier so that diffraction occurs.

Which combination of vibration frequency and gap width will produce the smallest angle of diffraction?
questions.explanation:
Diffraction angle depends on $\lambda/x$; smaller ratio gives less spreading. Wave speed is fixed, so $\lambda=v/f$: doubling $f$ halves $\lambda$. Choosing $2f$ (smallest $\lambda$) and $2x$ (widest gap) gives the smallest $\lambda/x$.

B is tempting because of the wide gap, but halving $f$ doubles the wavelength.

questions.text:
An outdoor concert has two large speakers beside the stage for broadcasting music.

In order to test the speakers, they are made to emit sound of the same wavelength and the same amplitude.

The curved lines in the diagram represent wavefronts.

Where is the loudest sound heard?
questions.explanation:
Loudest sound occurs where wavefronts (crests) from both speakers coincide, giving constructive interference. Point D lies on the intersection of a wavefront from each speaker.

The other points lie on a wavefront from only one speaker or between wavefronts, so waves there are not both at a crest; A and B look close to intersections but are not on both.

questions.text:
The equation

$\lambda=\dfrac{d\sin\theta}{n}$

is used to calculate the wavelength $\lambda$ of light in an experiment that uses a diffraction grating. The light from the diffraction grating is displayed on a screen.

What do the symbols $n$ and $d$ represent?

options.A: number of slits in the grating | distance between adjacent slits in the grating
options.B: number of slits in the grating | distance from grating to screen
options.C: order of intensity maximum | distance between adjacent slits in the grating
options.D: order of intensity maximum | distance from grating to screen

questions.explanation:
The grating equation $d\sin\theta=n\lambda$ comes from the path difference $d\sin\theta$ between adjacent slits being a whole number $n$ of wavelengths. So $d$ is the slit spacing and $n$ is the order of the maximum.

D is tempting from Young's fringes formula, where $D$ is screen distance, but that does not appear here.

questions.text:
The diagram shows a metal block.

The block has sides of length $a$, $b$ and $c$ as shown, and its volume is $V$. Each charge carrier has a charge $-q$ and the number density of the charge carriers in the metal is $n$. It takes each charge carrier an average time of $t$ to pass through the block.

What is an expression for the current $I$?
questions.explanation:
Total carriers in block $=nV$, total charge $nVq$. All this charge passes through in time $t$, so $I=Q/t=nqV/t$.

Equivalently $I=nAvq$ with $v=L/t$ gives $nq(AL)/t=nqV/t$. C omits the length along the current direction.

questions.text:
The circuit diagrams show two lamps X and Y each connected to a cell. The current in lamp X is $0.50\,\text{A}$ and its resistance is $9.6\,\Omega$. The current in lamp Y is $3.0\,\text{A}$ and its resistance is $1.2\,\Omega$.

What is the ratio $\dfrac{\text{power in lamp X}}{\text{power in lamp Y}}$?

The intensity of light incident on a light-dependent resistor (LDR) is increased. The temperature of a thermistor is increased. In each case, the current in the component is maintained at a constant value.

What happens to the potential difference across each component?
questions.explanation:
LDR resistance falls as light intensity rises; NTC thermistor resistance falls as temperature rises. With constant current, $V=IR$, so both p.d.s decrease.

Tempting C assumes the thermistor resistance rises with temperature, which is not the case for an NTC thermistor.

questions.text:
An iron wire has length 8.0 m and diameter 0.50 mm. The wire has resistance $R$.

A second iron wire has length 2.0 m and diameter 1.0 mm.

What is the resistance of the second wire?
questions.explanation:
$R=\rho L/A$. Length is ×1/4. Diameter doubles, so area ×4. New resistance $=R\times\frac{1}{4}\times\frac{1}{4}=R/16$.

B results from treating area as proportional to diameter rather than diameter squared.

questions.text:
A cell with constant electromotive force (e.m.f.) is connected across a fixed resistor. Over time, the internal resistance of the cell increases.

Which change occurs as the internal resistance of the cell increases?

options.A: a decrease in the charge of each charge carrier
options.B: a decrease in the potential difference measured across the cell
options.C: an increase in the energy dissipated per unit time in the fixed resistor
options.D: an increase in the number of charge carriers leaving the cell per unit time

questions.explanation:
$I=E/(R+r)$ falls as $r$ increases. The terminal p.d. $V=IR$ therefore falls too.

C and D are both wrong because a smaller current means less power in the resistor and fewer carriers leaving the cell per second.

questions.text:
Kirchhoff’s first and second laws are consequences of the conservation of different quantities.

What are those quantities?

options.A: first law: charge | second law: energy
options.B: first law: energy | second law: current
options.C: first law: current | second law: charge
options.D: first law: energy | second law: charge

questions.explanation:
The first law (currents at a junction) follows from conservation of charge. The second law (sum of e.m.f.s equals sum of p.d.s around a loop) follows from conservation of energy.

C is tempting, but current is not itself a conserved quantity.

questions.text:
A potentiometer circuit is used to determine the electromotive force (e.m.f.) $E_X$ of a cell. The circuit includes a second cell of known e.m.f. $E_0$ and negligible internal resistance, and a uniform resistance wire PQ of known length.

$E_X$ is less than $E_0$.

The movable connection J can be positioned anywhere along the length of the resistance wire.

Which circuit is suitable for determining $E_X$?
questions.explanation:
The driver cell $E_0$ must be connected across the full wire PQ. The test cell $E_X$ goes in series with the galvanometer between P and J, with like terminals facing so the p.d.s oppose. A balance point then exists because $E_X<E_0$.

The official answer is D, which by this criterion is the circuit with that arrangement. B and C are unsuitable because they place $E_X$ across the wire or the galvanometer in the driver loop.

questions.text:
In an experiment on $\alpha$-particle scattering, $\alpha$-particles are directed at a thin gold foil. Most of the $\alpha$-particles pass straight through the foil or are deflected by a small angle. A small number of $\alpha$-particles are deflected by a large angle.

Which statement **cannot** be deduced from this experiment?

options.B: Most of the mass of an atom is concentrated in the nucleus.
options.C: The nucleus of an atom contains protons.
options.D: The nucleus of an atom is small compared to the size of an atom.

questions.explanation:
Most particles passing straight through shows atoms are mostly empty space. Rare large deflections show a small, dense, charged nucleus holding most of the mass. The experiment shows the nucleus is positively charged but not that it contains protons, so C cannot be deduced.

B is tempting, but large deflections do require a massive nucleus.

questions.text:
Four nuclei are represented below.

$^{28}_{14}\text{E}$  $^{25}_{15}\text{G}$  $^{25}_{12}\text{M}$  $^{24}_{13}\text{Q}$

Which statement about these nuclei is correct?

options.A: An uncharged atom of element Q has 24 orbital electrons.
options.B: Nuclei G and M are isotopes of the same element.
options.C: When E absorbs a neutron and then emits an $\alpha$-particle, E transforms into M.
options.D: When M emits a $\beta^-$ particle, M transforms into Q.

questions.explanation:
For C: $^{28}_{14}\text{E}+n\to{}^{29}_{14}$, then losing an $\alpha$ gives $^{25}_{12}$, which is M. Correct.

A is wrong because Q has 13 electrons. B is wrong because G and M have different proton numbers. D is wrong because $\beta^-$ decay of M gives $^{25}_{13}$, not $^{24}_{13}$.

questions.text:
A neutron is composed of one up (u) quark and two down (d) quarks. When a neutron decays to a proton, a beta-particle is emitted.

What is the change in the quark structure of the neutron due to the emission of the beta-particle?

(The symbol for a neutrino is $\nu_e$ and for an antineutrino is $\overline{\nu}_e$.)
questions.explanation:
Neutron (udd) becomes proton (uud), so a d quark changes to a u quark. Charge is conserved: $-\tfrac13 = \tfrac23 - 1$. An electron is emitted, and lepton number conservation requires an electron antineutrino.

A wrongly uses a neutrino, which violates lepton number.

questions.text:
(a) In the following list, underline all units that are SI base units.

ampere     degree Celsius     kilogram     newton

(b) Fig. 1.1 shows a horizontal beam clamped at one end with a block attached to the other end.

[Fig. 1.1: horizontal beam held in a clamp at one end, block at the other end; arrow showing vertical direction of oscillations]

The block is made to oscillate vertically.

The Young modulus $E$ of the material of the beam is given by

$E = \dfrac{kM}{T^2}$

where $M$ is the mass of the block, $T$ is the period of the oscillations and $k$ is a constant.

A student determines the values and percentage uncertainties of $k$, $M$ and $T$. Table 1.1 lists the percentage uncertainties.

| quantity | percentage uncertainty |
|---|---|
| $k$ | ±2.1% |
| $M$ | ±0.6% |
| $T$ | ±1.5% |

The student uses the values of $k$, $M$ and $T$ to calculate the value of $E$ as $8.245\times10^{9}\,\text{Pa}$.

(b)(i) Calculate the percentage uncertainty in the value of $E$.

(b)(ii) Use your answer in (b)(i) to determine the value of $E$, with its absolute uncertainty, to an appropriate number of significant figures.

parts.label: (a)
parts.prompt:
In the following list, underline all units that are SI base units.

ampere     degree Celsius     kilogram     newton

parts.label: (b)(i)
parts.prompt: Calculate the percentage uncertainty in the value of $E$.

parts.label: (b)(ii)
parts.prompt:
Use your answer in (b)(i) to determine the value of $E$, with its absolute uncertainty, to an appropriate number of significant figures.

$E = (\ldots \pm \ldots)\times10^{9}\,\text{Pa}$
parts.mark_scheme:
absolute uncertainty = $(5.7/100)\times8.245\times10^{9}$ ($=4.7\times10^{8}$ Pa or $0.47\times10^{9}$ Pa) [1]
$E = (8.2\pm0.5)\times10^{9}$ Pa [1]

questions.subtopic: SI base units and propagation of uncertainties

questions.text:
A sphere is attached by a metal wire to the horizontal surface at the bottom of a river, as shown in Fig. 2.1.

The sphere is fully submerged and in equilibrium, with the wire at an angle of 68° to the horizontal surface. The weight of the sphere is 32N. The upthrust acting on the sphere is 280N. The density of the water is $1.0\times10^{3}\,\text{kg m}^{-3}$.

Assume that the force on the sphere due to the water flow is in a horizontal direction.

(a) By considering the components of force in the vertical direction, determine the tension in the wire.

(b) For the sphere, calculate:

(i) the volume

(ii) the density.

(c) The centre of the sphere is initially at a height of 6.2m above the horizontal surface. The speed of the water then increases, causing the sphere to move to a different position. This movement of the sphere causes its gravitational potential energy to decrease by 77J.

Calculate the final height of the centre of the sphere above the horizontal surface.

(d) The extension of the wire increases when the sphere changes position as described in (c). The wire obeys Hooke's law.

(i) State a symbol equation that gives the relationship between the tension $T$ in the wire and its extension $x$. Identify any other symbol that you use.

(ii) Before the sphere changed position, the initial elastic potential energy of the wire was 0.65J. The change in position of the sphere causes the extension of the wire to double.

Calculate the final elastic potential energy of the wire after the sphere has changed position.

parts.label: (a)
parts.prompt: By considering the components of force in the vertical direction, determine the tension in the wire.

parts.label: (b)(i)
parts.prompt: the volume

parts.label: (b)(ii)
parts.prompt: the density.

parts.label: (c)
parts.prompt: Calculate the final height of the centre of the sphere above the horizontal surface.
parts.mark_scheme:
$\Delta E = mg\Delta h$ or $\Delta E = W\Delta h$ [1]
$\Delta h = 77/32$ [1]
$\Delta h = 2.4$, final height $= 6.2 - 2.4 = 3.8\,\text{m}$ [1]
parts.model_answer:
$\Delta E = W\Delta h$, so $\Delta h = 77/32 = 2.4\,\text{m}$

Final height $= 6.2 - 2.4 = 3.8\,\text{m}$

parts.label: (d)(i)
parts.prompt: State a symbol equation that gives the relationship between the tension $T$ in the wire and its extension $x$. Identify any other symbol that you use.
parts.mark_scheme: $T = kx$ where $k$ is a constant, or $T=(EA/L)x$ where $A$ is cross-sectional area, $E$ is Young modulus, $L$ is original length [1]
parts.model_answer: $T = kx$, where $k$ is the spring constant of the wire.

Fig. 3.1 (not to scale)

On Fig. 3.2, sketch a graph to show the variation of the velocity $v$ of the ball with time $t$ from $t = 0$ to $t = T$. Numerical values of $v$ and $t$ are not required. Assume that $v$ is positive in the upward direction.

(d) State what is represented by the gradient of the graph in (c).

(e) The man now throws a second ball with the same velocity and from the same height as the first ball. The mass of the second ball is greater than that of the first ball. Assume that air resistance is still negligible.

For the first and second balls, compare:

(i) the magnitudes of their accelerations

(ii) the speeds with which they hit the ground.

a single sloping straight line drawn from $t = 0$ to $t = T$ [B1]
line starts with a positive non-zero value of $v$ and ends with a negative non-zero value of $v$ [B1]

questions.text:
(a) State the principle of conservation of momentum.

(b) Two balls, X and Y, move along a horizontal frictionless surface, as shown from above in Fig. 4.1.

Ball X has a mass of 3.0kg and a velocity of $4.0\,\text{m s}^{-1}$ in a direction at angle $\theta$ to a line AB. Ball Y has a mass of 2.5kg and a velocity of $4.8\,\text{m s}^{-1}$ in a direction at angle $\theta$ to the line AB.

The balls collide and stick together. After colliding, the balls have a velocity of $3.7\,\text{m s}^{-1}$ along the line AB on the horizontal surface, as shown in Fig. 4.2.

(b)(i) By considering the components of the momenta along the line AB, calculate $\theta$.

(b)(ii) By calculation of kinetic energies, state and explain whether the collision of the balls is inelastic or perfectly elastic.

parts.label: (a)
parts.prompt: State the principle of conservation of momentum.
parts.mark_scheme:
sum/total momentum before = sum/total momentum after or sum/total momentum (of a system of objects) is constant [1]
if no (resultant) external force/for a closed system [1]
parts.model_answer: The total momentum of a system of objects remains constant (total momentum before = total momentum after), provided no resultant external force acts on the system.

parts.label: (b)(i)
parts.prompt: By considering the components of the momenta along the line AB, calculate $\theta$.

parts.label: (b)(ii)
parts.prompt: By calculation of kinetic energies, state and explain whether the collision of the balls is inelastic or perfectly elastic.
parts.mark_scheme:
(initial $E_K=\frac{1}{2}\times3.0\times4.0^2+\frac{1}{2}\times2.5\times4.8^2=$) 53 (J) or (final $E_K=\frac{1}{2}\times5.5\times3.7^2=$) 38 (J) [1]
values of initial $E_K$ and final $E_K$ both correct **and** inelastic stated [1]
parts.model_answer:
Initial $E_K=\frac{1}{2}(3.0)(4.0)^2+\frac{1}{2}(2.5)(4.8)^2=24+28.8=53\,\text{J}$

Final $E_K=\frac{1}{2}(5.5)(3.7)^2=38\,\text{J}$

Kinetic energy decreases, so the collision is inelastic.

questions.text:
Light from a laser is used to produce an interference pattern on a screen, as shown in Fig. 5.1.

The light of wavelength 660 nm is incident normally on two slits that have a separation of 0.44 mm. The double slit is parallel to the screen. The perpendicular distance between the double slit and the screen is 1.8 m.

The central bright fringe on the screen is formed at point O. The next dark fringe below point O is formed at point P. The next bright fringe and the next dark fringe below point P are formed at points Q and R respectively.

(a) The light waves from the two slits are coherent.

State what is meant by coherent.

(b) For the two light waves superposing at R, calculate:

(i) the difference in their path lengths, in nm, from the slits

(ii) their phase difference.

(c) Calculate the distance OQ.

(d) The intensity of the light incident on the double slit is increased without changing the frequency.

Describe how the appearance of the fringes after this change is different from, and similar to, their appearance before the change.

(e) The light of wavelength 660 nm is now replaced by blue light from a laser.

State and explain the change, if any, that must be made to the separation of the two slits so that the fringe separation on the screen is the same as it was for light of wavelength 660 nm.

parts.label: (a)
parts.prompt:
The light waves from the two slits are coherent.

State what is meant by coherent.
parts.model_answer: The waves have a constant phase difference.

parts.label: (b)(i)
parts.prompt: For the two light waves superposing at R, calculate the difference in their path lengths, in nm, from the slits.
parts.model_answer: R is the second dark fringe, so path difference $= 1.5\lambda = 1.5 \times 660 = 990\,\text{nm}$.

parts.label: (b)(ii)
parts.prompt: For the two light waves superposing at R, calculate their phase difference.

parts.label: (c)
parts.prompt: Calculate the distance OQ.
parts.model_answer: OQ is one fringe spacing: $x = \lambda D/a = (660\times10^{-9}\times1.8)/(0.44\times10^{-3}) = 2.7\times10^{-3}\,\text{m}$.

parts.label: (d)
parts.prompt:
The intensity of the light incident on the double slit is increased without changing the frequency.

Describe how the appearance of the fringes after this change is different from, and similar to, their appearance before the change.
parts.mark_scheme:
bright fringes are brighter [1]
no change to dark fringes [1]
no change to (fringe) separation / (fringe) spacing [1]
parts.model_answer: The bright fringes become brighter. The dark fringes remain dark (unchanged). The fringe separation stays the same.

parts.label: (e)
parts.prompt:
The light of wavelength 660 nm is now replaced by blue light from a laser.

State and explain the change, if any, that must be made to the separation of the two slits so that the fringe separation on the screen is the same as it was for light of wavelength 660 nm.
parts.mark_scheme:
(blue light has) shorter wavelength [1]
(so) decrease (slit) separation [1]
parts.model_answer: Blue light has a shorter wavelength, and since $x = \lambda D/a$, the slit separation $a$ must be decreased to keep $x$ the same.

questions.text:
(a) A network of three resistors of resistances $R_1$, $R_2$ and $R_3$ is shown in Fig. 6.1.

[Fig. 6.1: three resistors $R_1$, $R_2$, $R_3$ in series carrying current $I$, with p.d.s $V_1$, $V_2$, $V_3$ across them and total p.d. $V$]

The individual potential differences across the resistors are $V_1$, $V_2$ and $V_3$. The current in the combination of resistors is $I$ and the total potential difference across the combination is $V$.

Show that the combined resistance $R$ of the network is given by

$R = R_1 + R_2 + R_3$. [2]

(b) A battery of electromotive force (e.m.f.) 8.0 V and negligible internal resistance is connected to a thermistor, a switch X and two fixed resistors, as shown in Fig. 6.2.

[Fig. 6.2: 8.0 V battery in series with $R_1$ (6.0 kΩ); $R_2$ (4.0 kΩ) in parallel with a branch containing switch X and a thermistor]

Resistor $R_1$ has resistance 6.0 kΩ and resistor $R_2$ has resistance 4.0 kΩ.

(i) Switch X is open.

Calculate the potential difference across $R_1$.

potential difference = ................ V [2]

(ii) Switch X is now closed. The resistance of the thermistor is 12.0 kΩ.

Calculate the current in the battery.

current = ................ A [2]

(c) The switch X in the circuit in (b) remains closed. The temperature of the thermistor decreases.

By reference to the current in the battery, state and explain the effect, if any, of the decrease in temperature on the power produced by the battery. [3]

parts.label: (a)
parts.prompt: Show that the combined resistance $R$ of the network is given by $R = R_1 + R_2 + R_3$.
parts.model_answer:
The total p.d. is the sum of the individual p.d.s: $V = V_1 + V_2 + V_3$.

The current $I$ is the same in each resistor, so using $V = IR$: $IR = IR_1 + IR_2 + IR_3$.

Dividing by $I$: $R = R_1 + R_2 + R_3$.

parts.label: (b)(i)
parts.prompt:
Switch X is open.

Calculate the potential difference across $R_1$.

parts.label: (b)(ii)
parts.prompt:
Switch X is now closed. The resistance of the thermistor is 12.0 kΩ.

Calculate the current in the battery.

parts.label: (c)
parts.prompt:
The switch X in the circuit in (b) remains closed. The temperature of the thermistor decreases.

By reference to the current in the battery, state and explain the effect, if any, of the decrease in temperature on the power produced by the battery.
parts.mark_scheme:
thermistor resistance increases [1]
(total resistance increases so) current (in battery) decreases [1]
($P = EI$ and $E$ constant so) power decreases [1]
parts.model_answer: As temperature falls, the thermistor's resistance increases, so the total circuit resistance increases and the current in the battery decreases. Since $P = EI$ with $E$ constant, the power produced by the battery decreases.

questions.text:
(a) A nucleus of caesium-137 ($^{137}_{55}\text{Cs}$) decays by emitting a $\beta^-$ particle to produce a nucleus of an element X and an antineutrino. The decay is represented by

$^{137}_{55}\text{Cs} \rightarrow\, ^{Q}_{S}\text{X} +\, ^{P}_{R}\beta^- +\, ^{0}_{0}\bar{\nu}$.

(a)(i) State the number represented by each of the following letters.

P ...

Q ...

R ...

S ...

(a)(ii) State the name of the class (group) of particles that includes the $\beta^-$ particle and the antineutrino.

(b) A particle Y has a quark composition of ddd where d represents a down quark.

A particle Z has a quark composition of $\bar{\text{u}}\text{d}$ where $\bar{\text{u}}$ represents an up antiquark.

(b)(i) Show that the charges of particles Y and Z are equal.

(b)(ii) State and explain which particle is a meson and which particle is a baryon.

meson: ...

baryon: ...

parts.label: (a)(i)
parts.prompt:
State the number represented by each of the following letters.

P ...

Q ...

R ...

S ...

parts.label: (a)(ii)
parts.prompt: State the name of the class (group) of particles that includes the $\beta^-$ particle and the antineutrino.

parts.label: (b)(i)
parts.prompt: Show that the charges of particles Y and Z are equal.
parts.model_answer:
Down quark charge $= -\frac{1}{3}e$; up antiquark charge $= -\frac{2}{3}e$.

Y (ddd): $-\frac{1}{3}e-\frac{1}{3}e-\frac{1}{3}e = -1e$

Z ($\bar{\text{u}}\text{d}$): $-\frac{2}{3}e-\frac{1}{3}e = -1e$

So both charges are $-e$, i.e. equal.

parts.label: (b)(ii)
parts.prompt:
State and explain which particle is a meson and which particle is a baryon.

meson: ...

baryon: ...
parts.mark_scheme:
meson: Z / $\bar{\text{u}}\text{d}$ because consists of a quark and an antiquark [1]
baryon: Y / ddd because consists of three quarks [1]
parts.model_answer:
meson: Z, because it consists of a quark and an antiquark.

baryon: Y, because it consists of three quarks.
